options.a: Inpatient hospital stays and skilled nursing facility care
options.b: Doctor visits and outpatient services received in a hospital
options.c: Long-term custodial care in a nursing home after a hospital stay
options.d: Outpatient prescription drugs dispensed at retail pharmacies

distractorExplanations.b: Physician visits and hospital outpatient services are Part B, even inside a hospital building; Part A covers inpatient care.
distractorExplanations.c: Medicare does not cover custodial care; Part A covers only limited skilled nursing facility care after a qualifying three-day inpatient stay.
distractorExplanations.d: Retail outpatient prescriptions are covered by Part D plans, not by Part A hospital insurance.

options.a: Long-term custodial care in a nursing home or assisted living facility
options.b: Physician services, outpatient care, preventive services, and DME
options.c: Routine hearing exams and hearing aids under Original Medicare
options.d: Inpatient hospital stays and skilled nursing facility care

distractorExplanations.a: No part of Medicare covers custodial care; it is paid privately, by long-term care insurance, or by Medicaid for those who qualify.
distractorExplanations.c: Original Medicare does not cover routine hearing exams or hearing aids; some Medicare Advantage plans offer them as an extra benefit.
distractorExplanations.d: Inpatient hospital and skilled nursing facility care are Part A benefits; Part B is the outpatient medical insurance.

options.a: Drugs given during an inpatient hospital stay
options.b: Medigap premiums and Original Medicare cost-sharing
options.c: Drugs a doctor administers by injection or infusion in the office
options.d: Outpatient prescription drugs through private plans

distractorExplanations.a: Drugs administered during a covered inpatient stay are part of the Part A hospital payment, not billed to a Part D plan.
distractorExplanations.b: Part D plans pay only for covered outpatient drugs; Medigap premiums and Part A/B cost-sharing are outside Part D.
distractorExplanations.c: Physician-administered injectables and infusions in the office are generally covered under Part B, not Part D.

options.a: Alternative way to receive Part A and B benefits through private plans
options.b: A supplement that pays the cost-sharing left over by Original Medicare
options.c: A government-run plan that replaces Part D drug coverage alone
options.d: A plan open only to people under 65 who qualify through disability

distractorExplanations.b: That describes Medigap, which works alongside Original Medicare; Medicare Advantage replaces how A and B benefits are delivered.
distractorExplanations.c: Medicare Advantage plans are run by Medicare-approved private companies and must cover all Part A and Part B benefits, often with drug coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: Anyone with Part A and Part B who lives in the plan’s service area can join, including people 65+ and, since 2021, people with ESRD.

options.a: Include outpatient drug coverage, so no separate Part D plan is needed
options.b: Help pay cost-sharing in Original Medicare, standardized in most states
options.c: Are sold by Medicare and work alongside a Medicare Advantage plan
options.d: Replace Original Medicare, with the insurer paying claims instead of Medicare

distractorExplanations.a: Medigap policies sold since January 1, 2006 cannot include drug coverage, so a separate Part D plan is needed for prescriptions.
distractorExplanations.c: Private insurers sell Medigap, and it cannot be sold to someone enrolled in Medicare Advantage because it only pays Original Medicare cost-sharing.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes Medicare Advantage; with Medigap, Original Medicare pays first and the policy pays its share of the remaining cost-sharing.

options.a: Any drug discount program that lowers the beneficiary’s pharmacy prices
options.b: Coverage with benefits identical in design to a standard Part D plan
options.c: Coverage that pays at least 50% of each prescription the beneficiary fills
options.d: Coverage expected to pay on average at least as much as standard Part D

distractorExplanations.a: Discount cards are not insurance and have no actuarial value; creditable coverage must be expected to pay at least as much as standard Part D.
distractorExplanations.b: Creditable status is an actuarial-value test; the plan’s deductible and copay design can differ from Part D as long as the expected value is equal or greater.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no fixed coinsurance threshold; creditable coverage is judged by expected value compared with standard Part D.

options.a: Medigap premiums and Part A deductibles for limited-income beneficiaries
options.b: Part B premiums and coinsurance paid through a state Medicare Savings Program
options.c: Part D premiums, deductibles, and copays for limited-income beneficiaries
options.d: Long-term care costs for beneficiaries who have used up their savings

distractorExplanations.a: Extra Help lowers Part D costs only; Medigap premiums are not covered, and Part A/B cost-sharing help comes from Medicare Savings Programs or Medicaid.
distractorExplanations.b: Paying Part B premiums and cost-sharing is a Medicare Savings Program (QMB/SLMB/QI) benefit, not the Part D Low-Income Subsidy.
distractorExplanations.d: Long-term care for people with very limited assets is a Medicaid benefit; Extra Help applies to Part D drug costs.

options.a: Curative treatment for the terminal illness alongside comfort care at no cost
options.b: Care for patients with a prognosis of twelve months or less, mainly in hospital
options.c: Custodial room and board in a nursing home for terminally ill patients
options.d: Comfort care for terminal illness with prognosis six months or less

distractorExplanations.a: After electing hospice, Medicare stops paying for treatment intended to cure the terminal illness; conditions unrelated to it remain covered.
distractorExplanations.b: Hospice eligibility requires a prognosis of six months or less, and care is usually delivered at home rather than in a hospital.
distractorExplanations.c: The hospice benefit does not pay room and board when a patient lives in a nursing home; it pays for hospice services delivered there.

options.a: Applies per benefit period, not calendar year only
options.b: Applies once per calendar year, like the Part B deductible
options.c: Applies once per lifetime, like the 60 lifetime reserve days
options.d: Applies per admission, even if readmitted within 60 days

distractorExplanations.b: The Part B deductible is annual, but the Part A inpatient deductible applies per benefit period and can be owed more than once a year.
distractorExplanations.c: Lifetime reserve days are a one-time pool of 60 days; the inpatient deductible recurs with each new benefit period.
distractorExplanations.d: A readmission within 60 days of discharge falls in the same benefit period, so no new Part A deductible is owed.

options.a: That Medicare Advantage costs less for most people, so it is the usual default
options.b: Which plan the counselor would personally choose given the beneficiary’s age
options.c: Network, cost-sharing, drug coverage, travel, and provider access differences
options.d: That Medigap can be bought later at any time without medical underwriting

distractorExplanations.a: Neutral counseling does not steer; a low premium can come with higher cost-sharing and network limits, so cost depends on the person’s use of care.
distractorExplanations.b: SHIP counselors give unbiased comparisons tied to the beneficiary’s needs, not personal recommendations based on age.
distractorExplanations.d: Medigap guaranteed-issue rights are limited to the open enrollment period and specific situations; in most states later applications can be underwritten.

options.a: Part D drug claims, plan payments, and the beneficiary’s copays
options.b: The amount the beneficiary owes Medicare, payable within 30 days
options.c: Medigap claims paid, remaining premium balance, and renewal dates
options.d: Services billed, Medicare-approved amounts, and beneficiary liability

distractorExplanations.a: Part D claims appear on the drug plan’s Explanation of Benefits; the MSN covers Original Medicare Part A and Part B claims.
distractorExplanations.b: The MSN is not a bill; it shows what may be owed to the provider, who bills the beneficiary separately.
distractorExplanations.c: Medigap insurers send their own statements; the MSN reports Original Medicare claims, approved amounts, and possible beneficiary liability.

options.a: Redetermination, reconsideration, ALJ hearing, and further review
options.b: Reconsideration, redetermination, ALJ hearing, and federal court
options.c: Redetermination, then binding arbitration, with no hearing available
options.d: A single Medicare Appeals Council review that is final

distractorExplanations.b: This swaps the first two levels: redetermination by the contractor comes first, then reconsideration by a Qualified Independent Contractor.
distractorExplanations.c: Medicare has no arbitration step; the third level is a hearing before an Administrative Law Judge, followed by Council and court review.
distractorExplanations.d: The Medicare Appeals Council is level four, after redetermination, reconsideration, and an ALJ hearing, and judicial review can follow it.

options.a: Request prior authorization from Medicare before the service is furnished
options.b: Inform beneficiary Medicare may not pay and obtain choice to receive service
options.c: Waive the beneficiary’s right to appeal if Medicare later denies the claim
options.d: Authorize a provider to change the diagnosis solely to obtain payment

distractorExplanations.a: An ABN is not a prior authorization request; it notifies the beneficiary of possible non-payment and records the choice to proceed and accept liability.
distractorExplanations.c: Signing an ABN does not waive appeal rights; the beneficiary can ask that the claim be submitted and appeal a denial.
distractorExplanations.d: Changing a diagnosis to get paid would be false billing; the ABN shifts financial liability only after honest notice of likely non-coverage.

options.a: Approval rights over every disclosure made for treatment or payment
options.b: Deletion of any record entry the beneficiary disagrees with
options.c: Access to records, accounting of disclosures, and complaint rights
options.d: A copy of the full record free of charge within 24 hours

distractorExplanations.a: HIPAA permits disclosures for treatment, payment, and operations without authorization; individuals may request restrictions but do not approve each one.
distractorExplanations.b: HIPAA gives a right to request amendment, not deletion, and the covered entity may deny the request with a written explanation.
distractorExplanations.d: Covered entities have 30 days (with one 30-day extension) to provide access and may charge a reasonable, cost-based fee.

options.a: A denied request for a service or payment the plan refused to cover
options.b: A dispute over the Part B premium amount set by Social Security
options.c: Disagreement with a drug formulary exception that was turned down
options.d: Quality of care or plan service issues not strictly payment denial

distractorExplanations.a: A refusal to cover a service or payment is an organization determination, which is challenged through an appeal, not a grievance.
distractorExplanations.b: Part B premium and IRMAA disputes go to Social Security, not to the Medicare Advantage plan’s grievance process.
distractorExplanations.c: A denied exception request is a coverage determination, so the remedy is a redetermination appeal, not a grievance.

options.a: Act with documented authorization in appeals and communications
options.b: Act for the beneficiary in appeals after a verbal request by phone
options.c: Make health care treatment decisions under the appeals form alone
options.d: Act as representative payee for the beneficiary’s Social Security checks

distractorExplanations.b: Appointing a representative requires a signed written appointment (form CMS-1696 or equivalent), not just a verbal request.
distractorExplanations.c: A CMS-1696 appointment covers claims and appeals; medical treatment decisions require a health care proxy or other legal authority under state law.
distractorExplanations.d: A representative payee is appointed separately by Social Security; a Medicare appointed representative does not manage benefit payments.

options.a: Allowed to charge up to 15% above the Medicare allowed amount
options.b: Generally prohibited from charging above Medicare allowed amount
options.c: Allowed to bill the beneficiary any amount Medigap does not pay
options.d: Prohibited from collecting the 20% Part B coinsurance from the patient

distractorExplanations.a: The 15% limiting charge applies to non-participating providers who do not accept assignment, not to participating providers.
distractorExplanations.c: Participating providers accept assignment, so the beneficiary owes only the Medicare deductible and coinsurance, not any remaining charge.
distractorExplanations.d: Participating providers do collect the Part B deductible and 20% coinsurance; what they cannot do is bill above the approved amount.

options.a: An appeal to the hospital’s own billing office within 30 days of discharge
options.b: Staying in the hospital free for 30 days while any appeal is pending
options.c: Notice of discharge rights and expedited appeal of discharge if applicable
options.d: A written discharge notice only if the stay lasted longer than 30 days

distractorExplanations.a: An expedited discharge appeal goes to the Beneficiary and Family Centered Care QIO, requested no later than the planned day of discharge.
distractorExplanations.b: Liability protection applies only while a timely QIO review is pending, which typically takes a day or two, not a fixed 30 days.
distractorExplanations.d: The Important Message from Medicare must be given to every Medicare inpatient within two days of admission and again before discharge.

options.a: Share the number with any caller who already knows your name and address
options.b: Give the number to callers offering free equipment if the doctor’s name is correct
options.c: Share the number with anyone who says they are calling from Medicare
options.d: Never share Medicare number except to trusted providers/plans; treat like SSN

distractorExplanations.a: Scammers often already hold personal details; knowing a name and address does not prove a caller is a legitimate provider or plan.
distractorExplanations.b: Equipment scams use real doctors’ names harvested from records; a correct doctor name does not make an unsolicited offer legitimate.
distractorExplanations.c: Medicare does not call to ask for a Medicare number unless the beneficiary called first; caller ID and claims can be faked.

options.a: Meaningful language access such as interpreters and translated materials
options.b: English materials, with a family member interpreting as the default
options.c: Counseling postponed until a bilingual counselor happens to be available
options.d: Translated materials only if the beneficiary pays the translation cost

distractorExplanations.b: Relying on family members as default interpreters is discouraged under Title VI and Section 1557 guidance; qualified interpreters should be offered.
distractorExplanations.c: Delaying service because of language can deny meaningful access; telephone or video interpreter services should be used instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Language assistance services must be provided free of charge to people with limited English proficiency.

options.a: Advance directives are a Medicare form filed with Social Security
options.b: Documents express care preferences; POLST/MOLST vary by state
options.c: A POLST replaces the health care proxy and applies in every state
options.d: Medicare requires an advance directive before a plan enrollment

distractorExplanations.a: Advance directives are state-law documents kept with the person, family, and providers; they are not Medicare or Social Security forms.
distractorExplanations.c: A POLST is a medical order for seriously ill patients that complements a proxy; its name, form, and recognition vary by state.
distractorExplanations.d: Under the Patient Self-Determination Act providers must inform patients about directives, but having one cannot be a condition of coverage or care.

medicare-counseling-readiness-check-righ.explanation: Counselors distinguish advance care planning documents from Medicare plan forms. Counseling should explain the applicable notice, deadline, privacy safeguard, and appeal or complaint pathway without promising an outcome. Advance directives are not the same as a Medicare enrollment form.

options.a: Deliver notice after services end, since appeals can only be filed afterward
options.b: Continue services until a federal ALJ hearing decides the appeal
options.c: Deliver standardized notice and continue services during appeal
options.d: Send the request to the plan’s grievance department for a 30-day review

distractorExplanations.a: The Notice of Medicare Non-Coverage must be delivered at least two days before services end so a fast-track appeal can be filed beforehand.
distractorExplanations.b: An ALJ hearing is the third appeal level; continuation applies during the fast-track QIO review, which is decided within days.
distractorExplanations.d: A termination-of-services appeal goes to the BFCC-QIO on a fast track; grievances handle service and quality complaints, not coverage termination.

medicare-counseling-readiness-check-righ.explanation: Expedited appeals have short timeframes; continuation of services may apply. Counseling should explain the applicable notice, deadline, privacy safeguard, and appeal or complaint pathway without promising an outcome. Continuation applies in qualifying situations when the fast-track appeal is filed on time.

options.a: Charging higher Part B premiums to higher-income beneficiaries
options.b: MA plans limiting enrollment to people living in the plan’s service area
options.c: Special Needs Plans enrolling only people with specific chronic conditions
options.d: Race, color, national origin, disability, age in federally funded programs

distractorExplanations.a: IRMAA is a lawful income-related premium adjustment set by statute; income is not a protected class under civil rights laws.
distractorExplanations.b: Service-area residence is a lawful Medicare Advantage eligibility requirement, not discrimination based on a protected characteristic.
distractorExplanations.c: Chronic-condition SNPs are designed by law to limit enrollment to qualifying conditions; that targeting is permitted, not prohibited discrimination.

options.a: Involve authorized representative/legal guardian per state law
options.b: Let the adult child who brought the beneficiary make the plan choice
options.c: Decide on the plan the counselor judges best, since no one else is present
options.d: Use the health care proxy to make insurance and financial decisions

distractorExplanations.b: Being a relative does not by itself confer legal authority; the person needs a power of attorney, guardianship, or authority under state surrogate law.
distractorExplanations.c: A counselor has no decision-making authority for a beneficiary; without a legal representative the counselor cannot choose for them.
distractorExplanations.d: A health care proxy covers medical decisions; insurance and financial choices generally need a financial power of attorney or guardian.

medicare-counseling-readiness-check-righ.explanation: Counseling respects legal decision-making authority and privacy rules. Counseling should explain the applicable notice, deadline, privacy safeguard, and appeal or complaint pathway without promising an outcome. Document the scope of the representative’s authority.

options.a: Recommends the plan with the highest star rating to every beneficiary
options.b: Does not sell insurance or receive marketing commissions from plans
options.c: May sell Medigap if the beneficiary declines Medicare Advantage options
options.d: Presents only the plans with no monthly premium to save the beneficiary money

distractorExplanations.a: Star ratings are one input; unbiased counseling compares plans against each person’s drugs, doctors, and costs rather than steering to one plan.
distractorExplanations.c: SHIP counselors do not sell any insurance product, including Medigap, and receive no commissions from plans.
distractorExplanations.d: A $0-premium plan can carry higher cost-sharing; unbiased counseling covers all relevant options, including Original Medicare with Medigap.

options.a: A provider billing a claim with an honest coding mistake later corrected
options.b: A beneficiary receiving a free preventive visit covered at 100%
options.c: Billing for services not provided or not medically necessary
options.d: A provider requiring a signed ABN before a non-covered service

distractorExplanations.a: An honest error that is corrected is an improper payment issue, not fraud, which requires knowingly false billing.
distractorExplanations.b: Many preventive services have no cost-sharing under Part B, so a $0 preventive visit is a normal covered benefit, not a scheme.
distractorExplanations.d: Obtaining an ABN before a likely non-covered service is the required, lawful practice, not a fraud scheme.

options.a: Give the caller the Medicare number only after the caller confirms the doctor’s name
options.b: Accept shipment first and ask whether it was ordered later
options.c: Pay a processing fee because Medicare never covers braces
options.d: Treat as potential scam; never give Medicare number; report suspicious contact

distractorExplanations.a: Equipment scammers obtain doctors’ names easily; confirming a name does not make an unsolicited caller legitimate or the order valid.
distractorExplanations.b: Accepting unordered equipment lets the supplier claim delivery and bill Medicare; the beneficiary should refuse it and check with the doctor.
distractorExplanations.c: Medicare can cover medically necessary braces ordered by a doctor; a fee demanded by an unsolicited caller is a scam tactic.

options.a: Advise reporting to SMP, Medicare, and reviewing MSN for unauthorized charges
options.b: Wait for the next MSN before acting, since supplies may have been ordered by the doctor
options.c: Tell the beneficiary to pay for the supplies so Medicare is not billed
options.d: Report only to the local police, since Medicare does not handle fraud complaints

distractorExplanations.b: Waiting lets more fraudulent claims accrue; the counselor should help report now and review existing claims online or on prior MSNs.
distractorExplanations.c: Paying the supplier does not stop misuse of a compromised number; the contact should be reported and claims reviewed.
distractorExplanations.d: Medicare, the Senior Medicare Patrol, and the HHS OIG hotline all accept fraud reports; police alone will not stop Medicare billing.

options.a: Legal discount fully compliant with AKS safe harbor when structured properly
options.b: Remuneration to induce referrals or use of services paid by federal programs
options.c: A billing error that overstates the units of a service on a claim
options.d: A plan offering a $0 premium to attract new members during enrollment

distractorExplanations.c: Overstated units are an improper or false claim issue; a kickback specifically involves remuneration to induce referrals or purchases.
distractorExplanations.d: A CMS-approved premium design is lawful plan pricing, not remuneration paid to induce referrals of federally funded services.
distractorExplanations.a: Compliant arrangements differ from inducements.

options.a: Bills separately for services that should be billed together as one code
options.b: Bills for services that were not actually provided to the patient
options.c: Bills higher level service code than documented care supports
options.d: Bills Medicare and a second payer for the same service

distractorExplanations.a: Splitting a bundled service into separate codes is unbundling, a related but different scheme from upcoding.
distractorExplanations.b: Billing for services not rendered is phantom billing; upcoding involves a real service billed at a higher level than documented.
distractorExplanations.d: Billing two payers for one service is duplicate or double billing, not upcoding to a higher-level code.

options.a: A claim showing a Medicare-approved amount lower than the billed amount
options.b: Separate claims from the hospital and the doctor for one surgery
options.c: A Part B deductible charge on the first claim of the year
options.d: Services in city beneficiary never visited during that period

distractorExplanations.a: Providers routinely bill more than Medicare approves; a lower approved amount is normal pricing, not a sign of identity theft.
distractorExplanations.b: Facility and professional services are billed separately, so two claims for one surgery are expected rather than suspicious.
distractorExplanations.c: The annual Part B deductible is normally applied to the first claims of the year, so this charge is expected.

options.a: 1-800-MEDICARE, SMP, HHS OIG hotline, or Medicare plan fraud line
options.b: The Social Security Administration’s retirement benefits office
options.c: The provider’s office manager, who forwards it to Medicare
options.d: The state Medicaid agency, since Medicare has no fraud hotline

distractorExplanations.b: Social Security handles enrollment and premiums; Medicare fraud is reported to 1-800-MEDICARE, the SMP, the OIG hotline, or the plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Reporting to the suspected provider alerts the subject and is not an official channel; reports go to Medicare, SMP, or OIG.
distractorExplanations.d: Medicare accepts fraud reports through 1-800-MEDICARE and the HHS OIG hotline; state Medicaid fraud units handle Medicaid matters.

options.a: Calling a beneficiary back after the beneficiary requested information
options.b: Door-to-door unsolicited contact prohibited in MA/Part D marketing rules
options.c: Hosting an educational event with neutral CMS content and no enrollment forms
options.d: Offering a promotional item of nominal value, worth under $15, at an event

distractorExplanations.a: Returning a call the beneficiary requested is permitted contact; the prohibition covers unsolicited door-to-door and similar outreach.
distractorExplanations.c: Educational events are allowed when they stay neutral and do not collect enrollment forms or sales information.
distractorExplanations.d: CMS allows promotional items of nominal value (currently up to $15 retail) offered to everyone regardless of enrollment.

options.a: Sign the receipt, then return the device to stop any Medicare charge
options.b: Accept it if the box lists the beneficiary’s own doctor as prescriber
options.c: Refuse if not ordered; document; check MSN; report if billed
options.d: Sign only after checking that the Medicare number on the label is correct

distractorExplanations.a: A signed delivery receipt can be used as proof of delivery to bill Medicare; returning the box later does not stop a fraudulent claim.
distractorExplanations.b: Fraudulent suppliers put real doctors’ names on orders; the beneficiary should confirm with the doctor before accepting anything.
distractorExplanations.d: A correct number means the supplier already has it; signing confirms delivery for billing instead of protecting the beneficiary.

options.a: Can still bill Medicare Advantage plans but not Original Medicare
options.b: Is barred from Medicaid in one state but may still bill Medicare
options.c: Can keep treating existing Medicare patients for up to two years
options.d: Cannot participate in federal healthcare programs

distractorExplanations.a: OIG exclusion covers every federal health care program, including Medicare Advantage plans and Medicaid, not just Original Medicare.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes a state Medicaid termination; an OIG exclusion is federal and bars Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal programs.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no grace period; federal programs will not pay for items or services furnished by an excluded provider from the effective date.

medicare-counseling-readiness-check-frau.explanation: LEIE providers/entities cannot furnish services paid by Medicare/Medicaid. The safe response is to protect the Medicare number, preserve records, review claims, and use official reporting channels. Billing federal programs for an excluded provider’s services is prohibited.

options.a: Do not click links; contact Medicare via official phone on card/website
options.b: Click the link but log in only if the page shows the Medicare logo
options.c: Reply to the email asking the sender to confirm it is really Medicare
options.d: Call the phone number listed in the email to verify the account

distractorExplanations.b: Phishing pages copy official logos; a familiar logo does not verify the site, so the link should not be used at all.
distractorExplanations.c: Replying confirms an active address to scammers; verification should go through the number on the Medicare card or Medicare.gov.
distractorExplanations.d: A number inside a phishing email reaches the scammer; use 1-800-MEDICARE or the number on the card instead.

options.a: Contact the provider directly to demand an explanation of the charges
options.b: Record facts objectively and refer to SMP without investigating
options.c: Wait until the beneficiary has three suspicious claims before referring
options.d: Collect the provider’s records to build the case before any referral

distractorExplanations.a: Confronting the provider can tip off a suspected fraudster and is outside the counselor’s role; the facts are referred to SMP.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no minimum number of suspicious claims; one questionable claim is enough to document and refer to SMP.
distractorExplanations.d: Gathering evidence from the provider is investigation, which belongs to SMP, the OIG, and law enforcement rather than the counselor.

options.a: Medicaid paying the Medicare cost-sharing for a QMB enrollee
options.b: Medicare paying first and Medicaid paying second on one claim
options.c: Billing both programs improperly for same service
options.d: A provider declining to bill a QMB enrollee for coinsurance

distractorExplanations.a: For Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries, Medicaid lawfully covers Medicare premiums and cost-sharing; that is proper coordination.
distractorExplanations.b: For dual eligibles Medicare is primary and Medicaid is payer of last resort, so this sequence is normal coordination of benefits.
distractorExplanations.d: Federal law prohibits billing QMB enrollees for Medicare cost-sharing, so declining to bill is required, not fraudulent.

options.a: Disputing charges and changing Medicare number if compromised
options.b: A refund from the SMP program for any fraudulent charges paid
options.c: Canceling Medicare enrollment and re-enrolling under a new SSN
options.d: Paying the charges now and requesting reimbursement from Medicare

distractorExplanations.b: The Senior Medicare Patrol helps beneficiaries report and resolve fraud but does not pay restitution for charges.
distractorExplanations.c: CMS can issue a new Medicare Beneficiary Identifier; enrollment is not cancelled and the Social Security number does not change.
distractorExplanations.d: Paying fraudulent charges validates them; the beneficiary should dispute the charges and report them instead.

options.a: Closed yes/no questions to quickly narrow the beneficiary’s options
options.b: Giving expert advice first, then confirming the beneficiary agrees
options.c: Open questions, affirmations, reflective listening, and summarizing
options.d: Pointing out the risks of each choice until the beneficiary decides

distractorExplanations.a: Motivational interviewing relies on open questions that invite the person to explain priorities; closed questions limit that exploration.
distractorExplanations.b: Leading with advice is the “righting reflex” that MI avoids; it elicits the person’s own reasons before offering information.
distractorExplanations.d: Pressing risks to push a decision is persuasion, which tends to raise resistance; MI uses reflective listening and summaries instead.

options.a: Cover every plan option in one session so nothing is left unexplained
options.b: Hand over the Medicare & You handbook and end the session
options.c: Recommend a single plan so the beneficiary does not have to choose
options.d: Prioritize issues, break information into chunks, and schedule follow-up

distractorExplanations.a: Covering everything at once causes cognitive overload; an overwhelmed beneficiary retains more when information is prioritized and chunked.
distractorExplanations.b: A handbook alone shifts the work to an overwhelmed person; pacing, priorities, and a follow-up plan are what help.
distractorExplanations.c: Choosing for the beneficiary breaks neutral counseling; the decision stays theirs, made at a manageable pace.

options.a: Explain in own words what they understood about next steps
options.b: Answer yes or no when asked whether they understood the information
options.c: Read the plan’s Summary of Benefits aloud back to the counselor
options.d: Repeat the counselor’s explanation word for word

distractorExplanations.b: Asking “Do you understand?” invites a polite yes; teach-back has the person explain in their own words so gaps become visible.
distractorExplanations.c: Reading a document aloud shows reading ability, not understanding of what the person must do next.
distractorExplanations.d: Rote repetition can happen without comprehension; teach-back asks for the person’s own words to check real understanding.

options.a: Beneficiary needs a Social Security retirement benefit estimate
options.b: Beneficiary needs free unbiased help comparing Medicare options
options.c: Beneficiary wants a licensed agent to recommend and sell a Medigap policy
options.d: Beneficiary needs Medicaid long-term care eligibility decided

distractorExplanations.a: Retirement benefit estimates come from Social Security; SHIP counsels on Medicare coverage choices.
distractorExplanations.c: SHIP does not sell insurance or act as an agent; a beneficiary wanting a sales agent is not seeking SHIP’s neutral help.
distractorExplanations.d: The state Medicaid agency decides eligibility; SHIP can explain programs and help apply but does not make that determination.

options.a: Include the counselor’s opinions on the beneficiary’s family situation
options.b: Be kept on the counselor’s personal device for quick follow-up
options.c: Be factual, minimal necessary PHI, stored securely per agency policy
options.d: Record only the plan chosen, leaving out advice and options discussed

distractorExplanations.a: Personal opinions about family are not factual case information and add unnecessary sensitive detail to the record.
distractorExplanations.b: Storing notes on a personal device moves PHI outside agency safeguards; records must be kept in approved, secure systems.
distractorExplanations.d: Notes should capture the options and advice given so follow-up is consistent and program reporting is accurate.

options.a: Drop employer coverage immediately without comparing coordination rules
options.b: Delay every part of Medicare, including premium-free Part A, because employment continues
options.c: Assume a spouse can remain on the employer plan without checking
options.d: Compare employer plan vs Medicare timing, Part B delay rules, and spouse coverage

distractorExplanations.a: Dropping active-employment coverage first can create gaps and lose benefits; Medicare coordination and employer size must be checked.
distractorExplanations.b: Premium-free Part A is usually worth taking at 65 (unless HSA contributions continue), and Part B delay depends on group coverage from current employment.
distractorExplanations.c: Spouse coverage depends on the employer plan’s rules once the worker becomes Medicare-eligible and must be confirmed.

options.a: Accept the gift if it is reported to the supervisor within 30 days
options.b: Decline or follow agency policy on nominal gifts to avoid undue influence
options.c: Accept it, since gifts are allowed once the counseling case is closed
options.d: Ask the beneficiary to give cash instead of the offered item

distractorExplanations.a: Reporting does not make an expensive gift acceptable; agency policy typically limits counselors to declining or nominal items only.
distractorExplanations.c: Closing a case does not remove the appearance of undue influence; agency gift rules still apply after counseling ends.
distractorExplanations.d: Cash creates the same conflict of interest as the gift and is typically prohibited by agency policy.

options.a: Learning standard facts about each culture to predict preferences
options.b: Treating every beneficiary identically to avoid any appearance of bias
options.c: Recognizing counselor does not know all cultural contexts
options.d: Matching each beneficiary with a counselor of the same background

distractorExplanations.a: Predicting preferences from cultural facts is a checklist approach that can stereotype; humility means asking the individual.
distractorExplanations.b: Identical treatment ignores individual values and context; Medicare rules stay the same, but how options are weighed differs by person.
distractorExplanations.d: Background matching is not humility and is often impossible; any counselor can practice humility by asking respectful questions.

medicare-counseling-readiness-check-coun.explanation: Humility supports respectful individualized counseling within same Medicare rules. SHIP-style counseling is free, neutral, beneficiary-centered, and documented according to the program’s privacy procedures. It also means asking respectful questions about the beneficiary’s values.

options.a: A verbal recap of next steps, since written summaries can expose PHI
options.b: Assurance that Extra Help approval follows once the form is submitted
options.c: Instructions to wait for Social Security or Medicaid to call before taking any step
options.d: Checklist of documents, agency contacts, deadlines, and scheduled follow-up call

distractorExplanations.a: A written action plan with minimal necessary information can be kept securely; verbal recaps alone lead to missed deadlines.
distractorExplanations.b: Social Security decides Extra Help eligibility; a counselor cannot assure approval and should plan for follow-up.
distractorExplanations.c: Applicants may need to respond to requests or check status; a proactive follow-up plan reduces missed deadlines.

options.a: Listen, validate emotion, explain appeal path, and offer practical next steps
options.b: Interrupt and tell the beneficiary that denials cannot be appealed
options.c: Promise the denial will be reversed before reviewing the notice
options.d: Advise filing a grievance with the plan, since that is how coverage denials are reversed

distractorExplanations.b: Interrupting escalates anger, and Medicare denials can be appealed through defined levels with deadlines on the notice.
distractorExplanations.c: A counselor cannot predict an appeal outcome; promising a reversal before reading the notice misleads the beneficiary.
distractorExplanations.d: Grievances address service and quality complaints; a coverage denial is challenged through the appeal process.

options.a: Group sessions may enroll attendees, while individual sessions only educate
options.b: Individual sessions follow a fixed script, while groups allow open questions
options.c: Group educates generally; individual addresses personal eligibility and choices
options.d: Group sessions may discuss attendees’ cases openly once they sign in

distractorExplanations.a: This reverses the roles: groups give general education, while personal eligibility and choices are handled one-on-one.
distractorExplanations.b: Individual counseling is tailored to the person’s questions and situation; scripted content fits general group education.
distractorExplanations.d: Signing an attendance sheet is not consent to share PHI; personal situations belong in confidential individual sessions.

options.a: Ask the beneficiary to enroll before leaving so the deadline is not missed
options.b: Close with the counselor’s recommended plan written on a card
options.c: End once questions stop, since summaries repeat what was already said
options.d: Summarize decisions/next steps and provide written resources

distractorExplanations.a: Pushing enrollment at closing is pressure; neutral counseling leaves the decision and timing to the beneficiary.
distractorExplanations.b: A personal plan recommendation breaks neutrality; closing summarizes the person’s own decisions and next steps.
distractorExplanations.c: A closing summary and teach-back reinforce understanding; silence does not mean the beneficiary has understood.

medicare-counseling-readiness-check-coun.explanation: Closure reinforces understanding and accessible follow-up within program rules. SHIP-style counseling is free, neutral, beneficiary-centered, and documented according to the program’s privacy procedures. Confirm how the beneficiary can reach the counselor with questions.
